title: IBM Business Automation Platform
summary: Led a portfolio-wide initiative to unify over a dozen individual product offerings into a single platform. Served as key liaison between product teams and executive stakeholders, overseeing five design teams and driving user-centered design thinking across the organization.

children.text: I led design across IBM's Business Automation portfolio, a dozen products accumulated over thirty years of acquisitions and countless additions, sold together but designed apart. The job was to turn the portfolio into a platform.

The main work was defining the information architecture and introducing new paradigms for how the products would work together. The central piece was something I called Projects: a unifying space that let the products interoperate, share a common mental model, and come together in a cohesive experience.
Years later, that unification work and that concept are still living in the product.

The project required working with senior VPs across competing business strategies, defining cross-portfolio direction, wrangling stakeholders, and directing design across five product teams. I was the senior advisory designer for the portfolio, overseeing the platform and its core experiences, with an advisory role to each team's design lead. Throughout, I advocated for design as the lens that could unify a portfolio that did not have much experience with design thinking before.

Two IBM sales teams once accidentally arrived at the same customer meeting, pitching competing products from our same portfolio. The story was told as a joke inside the organization, but it described the problem we were still facing.

The portfolio was the result of thirty years of acquisitions, re-orgs, and sprawl. Each product came with its own users, data models, interaction patterns, and a team whose internal incentives kept things siloed.

From the outside, customers saw unrelated experiences. Navigation diverged between products. A "task" meant something different in each one. From the inside, every cross-product workflow became an integration project, every shared concept needed a translation layer, and every new capability was hindered by old patterns. The easy became hard.

blocks.alt: Before-and-after portfolio diptych. Left: a crowded grid of inconsistent product tiles with different typography, logos, and navigation patterns. Right: the same capabilities organized into calm, cohesive swim lanes.
blocks.caption: The portfolio before and after consolidation — from a file cabinet of unrelated products to a coherent system.

children.text: Consolidation was already being pushed from multiple directions, and none of them lined up. IBM's Software Group wanted the portfolio pulled together into platforms called Paks. Business Automation leadership was running its own independent platform push. The product teams inside Business Automation were not interested. They had roadmaps of their own to hit. There was no internal alignment, just pressure from above and resistance from below.

Meanwhile, the portfolio was shifting underneath us. The target user was moving from central-IT specialists toward line-of-business. Adjacent platforms had their own roadmaps to coordinate with. The legacy products needed modernizing while new capabilities kept arriving. Any consolidation plan had to absorb all of this at once.
Three things I did had the biggest impact.

Product teams ran against the platform direction by default. Each had its own revenue targets, and cross-portfolio work always lost to local KPIs. Above me, a cross-platform design team was setting pattern vision without the constraints it was designing into. Design VPs had their own priorities. None of it cohered on its own.

I worked through the design leads embedded in each product team — carrying constraints up, bringing elegant solutions back down from the executive stakeholder, and coordinating laterally with adjacent platforms to keep the picture coherent. Design played the facilitator and guide role the org otherwise lacked.

blocks.alt: Three-layer stack diagram showing the cross-platform design team at top, the platform initiative in the middle, and product teams at the bottom, with up/down arrows through the middle and lateral arrows to adjacent platforms.
blocks.caption: The connective role: carrying constraints up from product teams, bringing solutions back down from executive stakeholders, and coordinating laterally with adjacent platforms.

children.text: The competing pushes, the shifting user base, and the product-level misalignment formed a mess no single stakeholder could see whole. Design could, so I articulated the real problem space: what was actually broken, where the seams had to go, and what the target state needed to look like. That articulation was what made solutions possible.

Products across the portfolio used different words for the same concepts, and the same words for different concepts. Rather than negotiate vocabulary upfront, I worked at the level underneath: defining the objects and their relationships, then extending the model where the existing concepts fell short. The largest of those extensions was projects.
The moves shared one question.

blocks.text: How do we design and articulate what the system ought to be, then negotiate and build the path to it?

children.text: My solution was Projects, a concept I prototyped and pitched across the org. A project is a container for collaborative work, organized around an initiative. It became the central concept across the portfolio and the synthesis that unified the landscape. Inside a project, assets authored by each tool in the platform — forms, processes, decisions, cases, documents — reference each other natively. A form from one product calls a process from another without glue code. Teams have one entry point instead of a branching decision about which product to open first.
Projects became the foundation. Everything else followed from them.
Five decisions defined how a project worked, what lived inside it, and how it connected to the rest of the platform.

tiles.title: Three levels of structure
tiles.body: Project is the container, typed by domain. Asset is the user-generated object — forms, processes, decisions, cases, documents. Artifact is the reusable building block — templates, toolkits, components — that gets pulled into assets.

tiles.title: Tailored authoring
tiles.body: Each pillar contributes its own project tooling: App, Workflow, Decision, Digital Worker, Content, Data. The container is shared; the experience inside is tuned to the domain. Specialists still get the bespoke environment their work demands, just inside one platform.

tiles.title: Repository-backed
tiles.body: Every project lives in a Git-backed repository. Versioning, branching, and sharing happen at the repository level. Authoring aligned with modern developer workflows while still supporting citizen developers.

tiles.title: Three-container lifecycle
tiles.body: Projects for authoring, where assets are built. Asset Catalogs for discovery and reuse. Deployment Spaces for runtime, where assets are published for execution.

tiles.title: Designers as microservices
tiles.body: Each pillar's authoring environment registers as a microservice. A central Resource Registry makes the ecosystem extensible — new authoring tools plug in without rewriting the shell.

blocks.alt: Object model diagram. A Project container at center holds Asset boxes (form, process, decision, case, content) with Artifact tokens feeding into them. Surrounding the project is a left-to-right lifecycle: Projects (author) → Asset Catalogs (share) → Deployment Spaces (run). Typed-project labels (App, Workflow, Decision, Digital Worker, Content, Data) ring the edge.
blocks.caption: The IA decisions in one frame: container, asset hierarchy, three-container lifecycle, and typed projects as variants of one shape.

items.body: One place where different products' assets reference each other and work together.
Shared primitives — tasks, actions, properties, forms, services — across products.
Start a project, pull in whichever tools you need.
A specialist user moves beyond their silo because adjacent capabilities are reachable inside the container.
A shared surface for work that spans tools and roles.
New capabilities plug into the same container rather than spawning parallel product shells. Automation and intelligence asset types emerged this way.

children.text: The past reality was specialist-driven. Central IT and legacy teams ran the deep work; bandwidth was always the bottleneck. Line-of-business users didn't know how to get help, didn't want to wait for capacity, and didn't get on the roadmap. Along with new low-code tooling, the project container shifted that. LoB users could build solutions for themselves, pulling in shared artifacts or coordinating with specialists as the work required.
Each paired with what the same work looked like before, when it happened at all.

items.body: Often done manually, or not built at all because the cross-product integration cost wasn't worth it. The technical path required a workflow in the workflow tool, a digital worker agent in the automation tool, a content service for classification through a separate product, and a human-review app in yet another product, stitched together with custom integration code and manual context handoffs between runtimes.
A workflow, a digital worker task, a content service skill, and a human-review app compose natively. One mental model, one object model, one deployment surface.

Often handled by a specialist team piecing steps together manually, or not attempted at all because the integration cost was prohibitive. The integrated path required sponsorship rules in the decisions tool, resume extraction in the document processing tool, tiering in the decisions tool again, and routing in the workflow tool. Each authored in its own environment, deployed separately, and integrated by hand.
Decision, content, decision, and workflow compose inside one project. Assets reference each other natively. The whole hiring lifecycle is one thing the user designs, deploys, and reasons about.

blocks.alt: Before-and-after flows for two scenarios. Left frames: four disconnected tool boxes with messy arrows, glue-code labels, and handoff markers. Right frames: one project container with four assets nested inside, referencing each other natively.
blocks.caption: Email routing and HR hiring, before and inside a project — what moved from integration code into the object model.

children.text: The pattern the two flows expose: cross-pillar composition moved from a systems-integration problem to a design problem. Beyond that, the container let flows exist that otherwise would not have been built at all. The integration cost was no longer the gate.
Design only helps users once it ships. The rest of the work was championing the concept, aligning the puzzle pieces, leading the design teams that built it, and seeing it through to delivery.

I made the case through mockups, concept decks, and iterative playbacks. Every VP, product lead, and design team got a tangible object to react to, commit to, or debate. Skeptics became sponsors once they could see their product's capabilities plugging in.

blocks.alt: Concept artifacts gallery — four pieces showing the progression of the unifying concept: an early Solutions Concept hero slide, a proposed architecture diagram, a Projects kickoff deliverable, and an experience-based roadmap.
blocks.caption: The concept evolving across mockups, concept decks, architecture diagrams, and experience-based roadmaps — each one a tangible object stakeholders could react to.

children.text: Before the teams could build in parallel, they had to be working with the same puzzle pieces. I aligned IA and taxonomy across the portfolio — the object model, the common vocabulary, the shared structure — so every team shared the same definitions. Once the pieces were aligned, the teams could build on top of them instead of negotiating integration from scratch each time.

I was the point person across the five design teams that built the concept out. I kept rallying them around the vision and was hands-on helping the other design leads work through their team's version of the problem. I understood each team's core product goals and the tensions they were working through, and proposed solutions that held up across products. I often understood the crux of a product better than its own lead did.

blocks.alt: Portfolio architecture diagram. The shared Projects container at center, with each design team's authoring surface plugging in as a contribution. A perimeter band marks the cross-team design leadership scope.
blocks.caption: One portfolio, one shared container, five teams contributing — and the cross-team design leadership scope marked around the whole.

children.text: I worked with the teams to prioritize, plan, and set up sprints against the vision so they could execute it. The concept got adopted, built, and landed in the product. Teams that had been skeptical were shipping inside the shared container. What I'd been championing became the default.

blocks.alt: Shipped product gallery — four frames showing the consolidated platform in production: the Business Automation Studio with the Projects container, a workflow authoring surface, a decision authoring surface, and a build-flow sequence inside a project.
blocks.caption: The concept in the shipped product: shared container, pillar-tuned authoring surfaces, and an end-to-end build flow inside one project.

children.text: We were able to successfully ship Projects and impact real users. Tools that moved into the platform and adopted the shared object model went on to show measurable impact.

A Forrester Total Economic Impact study in 2022 found that customers running on IBM Cloud Pak for Business Automation realized substantial returns and gains in productivity. The platform being studied was the consolidated one — the object model, the container, the shared authoring surface that came out of this work.

blocks.label: ROI over three years.
blocks.source: Forrester Total Economic Impact study of IBM Cloud Pak for Business Automation, July 2022

children.text: Customers running cross-pillar work inside the container reported concrete outcomes. Tools that had once been separate products were now working together inside one project, shipped by one team, deployed as one thing.

trade promotions executed annually across 60,000+ dealers.

blocks.title: Pillars that plugged in became industry leaders

children.text: Operational Decision Manager — a pillar that plugged into the container as a microservice — was named a Leader in Forrester's most recent evaluation of AI Decisioning Platforms. Integration sharpened each pillar: the container handled what was shared, and the pillars were free to go deeper on what was unique.

blocks.label: Forrester Wave™: AI Decisioning Platforms, Q2 2025.
blocks.source: IBM Operational Decision Manager, the Decisions pillar of the consolidated platform

children.text: This was an ambitious, hard-fought design endeavor, and one that was very rewarding as a designer. Setting vision, directing teams, and collaborating cross-discipline is my favorite part of the profession. The results speak for themselves.

blocks.text: The senior designer's job is to shape the direction, not just execute on it. A good concept can carry more weight than any plan, if you can convince people to live inside it.
